question: H1
answer:
ANSWER

A US airline operating under FAA Part 121 (domestic, flag, or supplemental operations) must give a flight attendant a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours between the completion of one scheduled duty period and the commencement of the next, when the flight attendant is scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less. 14 CFR 121.467(b)(2). That 10 hours is a hard floor: it 'may not be reduced to less than 10 consecutive hours' under any circumstances. 121.467(b)(3).

Headline figure: 10 consecutive hours (regulatory minimum; airline policy or a collective bargaining agreement may be more generous).

---

1. REGULATORY BASIS AND SCOPE

- Rule: 14 CFR 121.467, 'Flight attendant duty period limitations and rest requirements: Domestic, flag, and supplemental operations.'
- Applies to certificate holders conducting domestic, flag, or supplemental operations under Part 121 (i.e., US scheduled airlines and the flag/supplemental operations of those carriers). It does not by its terms set the rule for Part 135 commuter/on-demand operators, foreign air carriers, or Part 91 operations.
- 'Rest period' is defined in 121.467(a) as 'the period free of all restraint or duty for a certificate holder conducting domestic, flag, or supplemental operations and free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise.'
- No carrier may assign a flight attendant any duty period unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required by the section: 121.467(b)(10). No carrier may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty during a required rest period: 121.467(b)(11).

2. REST REQUIRED, BY DUTY-PERIOD LENGTH

| Scheduled duty period | Required rest between duty periods | Cite |
|---|---|---|
| 14 hours or less | At least 10 consecutive hours; not reducible | 121.467(b)(1), (b)(2), (b)(3) |
| More than 14 hours, up to 16 (requires at least one flight attendant above the minimum complement) | At least 12 consecutive hours | 121.467(b)(4), (b)(7) |
| More than 16 hours (further additional-flight-attendant conditions in (b)(5)) and the extended operations covered by (b)(6) | At least 12 consecutive hours | 121.467(b)(5), (b)(6), (b)(7) |
| Any of the above over-14-hour cases | The 12 hours may be scheduled or reduced to 10 consecutive hours only if the flight attendant is given a subsequent rest of at least 14 consecutive hours, scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest, and occurring between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the next one | 121.467(b)(8) |
| Following a reduced-rest election under (b)(8) | The carrier may not schedule the flight attendant for a duty period of more than 14 hours during the 24-hour period commencing after the beginning of the reduced rest period | 121.467(b)(9) |

Practical reading: 10 hours is the universal floor; 12 hours is the requirement whenever the carrier uses the extended duty-period provisions above 14 hours, and even then it may come down to 10 only by pairing it with a 14-hour compensatory rest within 24 hours and a 14-hour duty cap on the following day.

3. SEPARATE, NON-INTERCHANGEABLE REQUIREMENT: 24-IN-7

Independently of the between-duty-days rest, each carrier must relieve each flight attendant from all further duty for at least 24 consecutive hours during any 7 consecutive calendar days. 121.467(b)(13). This is a weekly rest-free block, not a substitute for the daily 10 hours, and the 10 hours does not satisfy it.

4. WHAT DOES NOT COUNT AS REST

Time spent in transportation, not local in character, that the carrier requires and provides to move the flight attendant to an airport where he or she will serve as a crewmember, or from an airport where the flight attendant was relieved from duty back to the home station, is not part of a rest period. 121.467(b)(12). Practical consequences:
- A hotel-to-airport van or a company-arranged long-positioning segment inside what would otherwise be the rest window eats into the 10 hours; the 10 hours must be rest that is actually free of that transportation.
- Local transportation (e.g., hotel shuttle of a local character at a layover station) is not excluded by the text of (b)(12); the exclusion is aimed at non-local transportation. Document the characterization in the carrier's manual.
- Deadheading that is assigned duty is duty, not rest.

5. SCHEDULED VERSUS ACTUAL, AND IRREGULAR OPERATIONS

- The regulation is written in terms of what the carrier may assign/schedule: a 'scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours' measured from completion of the scheduled duty period to commencement of the subsequent scheduled duty period. 121.467(b)(2).
- Overrun protection in (b)(14): a flight attendant is not considered scheduled in excess of the duty-period limitation if the flights were scheduled and normally would terminate within the limits but, due to circumstances beyond the carrier's control (e.g., adverse weather), were not expected at departure to reach destination within the scheduled time.
- Critically, (b)(3) removes any reduced-rest escape valve for the 14-hours-or-less case, and the 2022 final rule implementing section 335(a) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 states the requirement that the 10-hour rest 'is not reduced under any circumstances' with no waiver permitted. Airlines cannot contract, schedule, or obtain flight-attendant consent around the 10 hours. Where an actual delay erodes rest below 10 hours, the flight attendant is not legal for the next duty period until 10 consecutive hours of rest have been received; the fix is delay/cancel/reassign the flying, not reduce the rest.
- The 12-to-10 reduction in (b)(8) is the only reduction mechanism in the section, it applies only to the over-14-hour duty cases, and it carries the 14-hour compensatory rest and the (b)(9) duty cap.

6. HISTORY / CURRENCY (why older numbers you may see are wrong)

Before the 2022 final rule, 121.467(b)(2) required 9 consecutive hours, and the carrier could schedule or reduce rest to 8 consecutive hours with a subsequent 10-hour rest beginning within 24 hours. The FAA's final rule 'Flight Attendant Duty Period Limitations and Rest Requirements' (ARM-220928-001, October 4, 2022), issued under section 335(a) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018, raised the minimum to 10 consecutive hours and eliminated reduction/waiver for the 14-hours-or-less case. The 2024 and 2025 CFR volumes and the current eCFR all show the 10-hour text. Any answer of 8 or 9 hours is superseded. Confirm currency against eCFR 14 CFR 121.467 before relying on this in an ops manual or a training document.

7. CAVEATS A REGULATORY SPECIALIST SHOULD FLAG

- Contract/Policy override upward only: a collective bargaining agreement or company policy may provide more rest (many carriers already schedule 10 hours, and some provide more). The regulation is a floor; the answer above is the regulatory minimum, not any particular carrier's practice. Check the applicable CBA for greater rest, different trip-construction rules, and reserve provisions.
- Part 117 election: 121.467(c) permits a carrier, with written procedures meeting the stated conditions, to apply the Part 117 flightcrew flight-time/duty/rest regime to its flight attendants instead. If a carrier has made that election, the Part 117 rest provisions govern and must be checked on their own terms; they are not the same as the 10-hour flight-attendant minimum. Do not assume the 10-hour answer for such a carrier without verifying the election and the Part 117 text.
- Reserve/on-call: reserve availability is duty or a duty-adjacent status under the carrier's FAA-approved program; the 10-hour rest obligation still runs between duty periods, but how reserve windows, short-call assignments, and airport alert interact with rest computation is carrier-program- and CBA-specific. Verify against the carrier's operations specifications/manual.
- International/flag: flag operations are covered by 121.467 itself, so the 10-hour floor applies to flag flying under Part 121 as well; foreign carriers and foreign-law rest rules are outside this section.
- Measurement conventions: compute from actual release (completion of duty) to actual report (commencement of the next duty), not from scheduled block times, when testing actual legality; use scheduled times when testing the schedule as constructed.

8. COMPLIANCE TEST (how to apply it)

For each pairing of consecutive duty periods:
1. Determine the scheduled length of the preceding duty period (report to release).
2. If <= 14.0 hours: required rest = 10.0 consecutive hours. No reduction permitted. Fail if rest < 10.0.
3. If > 14.0 hours (and the (b)(4)/(b)(5)/(b)(6) conditions, including the additional flight attendant, are documented): required rest = 12.0 consecutive hours, unless the carrier elects the (b)(8) reduction, in which case rest = 10.0 hours AND a subsequent rest of >= 14.0 consecutive hours begins no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest AND no duty period > 14.0 hours is scheduled in the 24 hours commencing at the start of the reduced rest.
4. Subtract from the rest window any non-local transportation the carrier requires and provides under (b)(12); the remaining time must still be >= the applicable minimum above.
5. Separately verify >= 24 consecutive hours free from all duty in each 7 consecutive calendar days under (b)(13).

9. ONE-LINE ANSWER

Ten consecutive hours of rest between duty days — 14 CFR 121.467(b)(2)-(b)(3) — not reducible, for a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less; twelve consecutive hours under (b)(7) where the carrier uses the extended duty-period provisions above 14 hours, reducible to ten only with the (b)(8) 14-hour compensatory rest and the (b)(9) duty cap.

answer:
# Maximum weight for an FAA 'small drone'

## Answer

**Less than 55 pounds (lb) on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.** 55 lb = 24.9476 kg = 880 oz.

The limit is **strict**: an aircraft weighing exactly 55.00 lb is **not** a small unmanned aircraft. A compliant aircraft weighs 54.99 lb or less. For design purposes, treat 55 lb as a hard ceiling and design to a demonstrated maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) below it (see §7).

Note on terminology: the FAA does not use 'small drone' as a term of art. The regulatory term is **small unmanned aircraft**, and the system-level term is **small unmanned aircraft system (sUAS)**. The 55 lb figure is the definition of the aircraft, not of the system.

## 1. Controlling regulatory text

| Source | Text |
|---|---|
| 14 CFR 107.3 (Definitions) | "**Small unmanned aircraft** means an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft." |
| 14 CFR 107.1(a) | Part 107 applies to "the registration, airman certification, and operation of civil small unmanned aircraft systems within the United States." |
| AC 107-2 §4.2.6 | "Small Unmanned Aircraft (UA). A UA weighing less than 55 pounds, including everything that is onboard or otherwise attached to the aircraft, and can be flown without the possibility of direct human intervention from within or on the aircraft." |
| FAA Part 107 Summary | "Unmanned aircraft must weigh less than 55 lbs. (25 kg)." |
| FAA AIP ENR 8.2 ¶2 | "UAS weighing 55 pounds MGOW or more must be registered under 14 CFR Part 47 ... UAS less than 55 pounds may be registered under the FAA's newer 14 CFR Part 48 online system." |

The 55 lb line is used consistently across Part 107 operations, Part 48/Part 47 registration, and the 49 U.S.C. 44809 recreational exception. There is no separate FAA 'large drone' weight class — above 55 lb the aircraft simply falls outside the small-UAS regime.

## 2. What the FAA weighs (and what it does not)

The definition is a **takeoff gross weight** — not empty weight, not net weight, not airframe-only weight. It is measured at the moment of takeoff.

**Counts toward the 55 lb:**

- Airframe, structure, landing gear, arms, booms
- Propulsion: motors, ESCs, propellers, shrouds/guards
- Energy source: all batteries at takeoff charge state, fuel, fuel tanks
- Avionics: flight controller, GNSS, IMUs, companion computer, radios, antennas
- Payload and cargo: cameras, gimbals, LiDAR, spray tanks and their contents, delivery packages, dispensers, winches
- Attached systems: parachute systems and launchers, recovery hardware, tethers and tether attachment hardware, lighting, strobes, external sensor pods
- Fasteners, ballast, trim weights, labels, paint, and any non-permanent additions present at takeoff

**Does NOT count toward the 55 lb:**

- The control station / ground control station (GCS), tablets, hand controllers
- Ground data terminals, ground antennas, tracking antennas, tripods
- Launch rails, catapults, nets, battery chargers, spares, tooling, cases
- Visual observer equipment

Rationale: 107.3 defines the weight limit on the *unmanned aircraft*; the control station and associated ground elements belong to the *system* (small UAS) definition and are not weighed against the 55 lb. This is a real design lever: move mass to the ground side (e.g., compute, high-gain antennas, batteries for a tethered GCS) and it does not consume aircraft mass budget. Anything that leaves the ground attached to the aircraft does.

**Timing:** the definition reads "on takeoff." Weight shed in flight (dropped payload, consumable spray, burned fuel) does not create compliance headroom — the aircraft must be under 55 lb at the instant of takeoff. (Contrast Category 1 over-people operations, which require 0.55 lb or less "on takeoff and throughout the duration of each operation," 14 CFR 107.110(a)(1).)

## 3. Unit traps that bite hardware teams

US rules are written in pounds. Metric BOMs and supplier specs invite two conversion errors that put an aircraft on the wrong side of the line:

| Common shorthand | Exact conversion | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "55 lb = 25 kg" | 55 lb = **24.9476 kg**; 25 kg = **55.1156 lb** | A 25.00 kg aircraft is **0.12 lb over** the limit and is **not** a small UA. Design ceiling in metric is **< 24.9476 kg**. |
| "0.55 lb = 250 g" | 0.55 lb = **249.476 g**; 250 g = **0.55116 lb** | A 250 g aircraft **exceeds** 0.55 lb. Category 1 / recreational registration design ceiling is **≤ 249 g**. |

Rule for the mass budget: carry the limit in **pounds** as the authority, convert to grams/kilograms only for the BOM, and round the *budget* toward compliance, never the limit.

## 4. Sub-thresholds below 55 lb (for context, not a substitute for the answer)

| Threshold | What it gates | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **0.55 lb (249.5 g)** | Category 1 operations over human beings (14 CFR 107.110); recreational registration | Cat 1 requires ≤0.55 lb on takeoff **and throughout the operation**, plus no exposed rotating parts that would lacerate skin. Recreational UAS >0.55 lb must be registered; ≤0.55 lb flown purely recreationally need not be. |
| **Any weight** | Part 107 registration | All UAS operated under Part 107 must be registered regardless of weight (14 CFR Part 48). |
| **55 lb** | Small UA definition; Part 48 vs Part 47 registration | <55 lb: small UA, Part 48 registration available. ≥55 lb: not a small UA; Part 47 aircraft registration. |

Categories 2 and 3 (operations over people) are **not** weight-gated beyond the 55 lb small-UA limit — they are gated by kinetic energy (Category 2 ≤11 ft·lb, Category 3 ≤25 ft·lb) and by declaration of compliance. Weight alone does not qualify or disqualify an aircraft for Cat 2/3.

Non-FAA weight classes sometimes mistaken for this answer: DoD Group 1 (≤20 lb), 'micro drone' (a marketing/DoD term, not FAA), and EASA's Open category subclasses (C0–C4, e.g. 250 g / 900 g / 4 kg / 25 kg) — none of these is the FAA rule.

## 5. What happens above 55 lb

Exceeding 55 lb removes the aircraft from the small-UAS regime entirely:

- **Part 107 no longer applies** — 107.1(a) is limited to civil small UAS. There is no weight waiver that converts a >55 lb aircraft into a Part 107 aircraft.
- Paths to legal flight become: a standard airworthiness certificate (Part 21) with operations under Part 91; an exemption under 49 U.S.C. 44807 (successor to Section 333) with a certificate of waiver or authorization; or public-aircraft operation under a COA.
- Registration moves to **14 CFR Part 47** (aircraft registration), not Part 48.
- Design consequences: airworthiness substantiation, continued airworthiness, and likely a formal certification basis — order-of-magnitude cost and schedule impact, not a paperwork delta.

## 6. Boundary behavior and enforcement reality

- **Exactly 55.00 lb is non-compliant.** The regulation says "less than 55 pounds." Do not design to equality.
- Scale uncertainty is real. A production scale readable to 0.01 lb with ±0.05 lb accuracy, plus build-to-build variation in batteries, paint, and fastener lots, can push a nominal 54.9 lb aircraft over. Reserve margin.
- The FAA does not approve a weight; the operator (remote PIC) is responsible for compliance. The practical exposure is a determination after an accident or inspection that the aircraft was over 55 lb, which voids the Part 107 basis for the entire operation.
- AC 107-2 requires the remote PIC to consider weight-and-balance limits and the consequences of an overweight aircraft; it explicitly notes that a published maximum gross takeoff weight may still need to be reduced for density altitude, launch area, wind, and obstacles. Regulatory compliance (under 55 lb) and safe performance (under the aircraft's own W&B limit) are two separate limits — the binding one is the lower.

## 7. Design guidance: mass budget targets

Recommended targets for a Part 107 aircraft (choose per risk tolerance):

| Target | Metric | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute regulatory ceiling | **< 24.9476 kg (55 lb)** | 14 CFR 107.3 |
| Design MTOW (recommended) | **≤ 24.5 kg (54.0 lb)** | ~1 lb margin for scale tolerance, configuration drift, added sensors, decals, repair doublers |
| Aggressive-margin design | **≤ 24.0 kg (52.9 lb)** | For long-life platforms with field-modifiable payloads |
| Category 1 over-people | **≤ 249 g (0.549 lb)** | 0.55 lb strict limit; 250 g fails |

Budgeting rule: allocate the 55 lb across airframe, propulsion, energy, avionics, and payload, and hold a named contingency line (2–4% of MTOW) that is *inside* the ceiling, not on top of it. Payload trade studies must be run against design MTOW, not against 55 lb.

For a cargo/package variant, note the separate Part 107 external-load constraint: the aircraft including attached systems, payload and cargo must weigh **less than 55 lb total**, the flight must be within visual line of sight, not from a moving vehicle or aircraft, and wholly within a single state (with the Hawaii / District of Columbia / territory carve-outs). The cargo mass is inside the 55 lb, not additive to it.

## 8. Verification procedure (how to prove the number)

1. **Define the maximum takeoff configuration** in the flight manual: airframe + props + batteries at maximum takeoff charge + all payload/cargo + attached sensors, parachute, antennas, tethers, labels. This configuration is the one that gets weighed.
2. **Weigh on a calibrated scale** — NTEP Class III / OIML Class III or better, resolution ≤0.01 lb (≤5 g), calibration certificate current within 12 months. Weigh in level attitude; for large multirotors weigh each landing-gear point on a matched set of pads and sum, or use a single platform rated ≥2× MTOW.
3. **Record** the result as Maximum Takeoff Weight in the flight manual and configuration record. Record it in pounds as the controlling unit, with kilograms in parentheses.
4. **Configuration control:** any change adding mass — new payload, larger battery, added sensor, paint scheme, repair doubler — triggers a re-weigh and a re-check against both the 55 lb regulatory ceiling and the aircraft's structural W&B limit.
5. **Operational check:** preflight procedure includes a go/no-go against the published MTOW, plus the AC 107-2 density-altitude/launch-site reduction check.

## 9. Scope caveats

- Applies to **US airspace and FAA jurisdiction** only. Other authorities set different limits (e.g., EASA Open category 25 kg MTOM, UK 25 kg, Canada 25 kg for advanced operations) — do not transfer the 55 lb figure.
- Current rule text as of the fetched 14 CFR (Part 107, incl. Amdt. 107-8, 86 FR 4381, Jan. 15, 2021). Verify against eCFR before certifying a design, since Part 107 has been amended repeatedly (notably the 2021 operations-over-people rule).
- The answer is the weight threshold only, not a full compliance analysis. Airworthiness, airspace authorization, remote pilot certification, and operations-over-people category requirements are separate gates.

answer:
BASIC VFR WEATHER MINIMUMS — CLASS E AIRSPACE BELOW 10,000 FT MSL

Governing rule: 14 CFR § 91.155(a), 'Basic VFR weather minimums' (current eCFR text; last amended by Amdt. 91-330A, 79 FR 41125, July 15, 2014). Corroborated by FAA AIM ¶ 3-1-4, Table 3-1-1, and FAA AIP ENR 1.4, Table ENR 1.4-1, which reproduce the same figures.

ANSWER

  Airspace:            Class E, less than 10,000 ft MSL
  Flight visibility:   3 statute miles
  Distance from clouds:
      Below clouds:     500 feet
      Above clouds:   1,000 feet
      Horizontal:     2,000 feet

Read as a single sentence: no person may operate an aircraft under VFR in Class E airspace below 10,000 ft MSL when the flight visibility is less than 3 statute miles, or when the aircraft is less than 500 ft below, less than 1,000 ft above, or less than 2,000 ft horizontally from any cloud.

KEY POINTS AND BOUNDARIES

1. It is 'flight visibility', not ground visibility, that the § 91.155(a) table prescribes. Ground visibility enters only through § 91.155(d), which applies inside the surface areas of Class B/C/D/E airspace designated for an airport (takeoff, landing, traffic pattern): 3 statute miles ground visibility, or 3 statute miles flight visibility if ground visibility is not reported.

2. The 10,000 ft MSL break is exclusive at the top of this regime. At or above 10,000 ft MSL in Class E the minimums step up to 5 statute miles visibility, 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, and 1 statute mile horizontal. The sub-10,000-ft answer above does not apply at or above 10,000 ft MSL.

3. Base-altitude rule — § 91.155(e): an aircraft operating at the base altitude of a Class E airspace area is considered to be within the airspace directly below that area. So an aircraft sitting exactly at the floor of a Class E layer uses the minimums of the airspace beneath, not those of the Class E layer above.

4. No day/night split. Unlike Class G, the Class E row of the § 91.155(a) table has no day-versus-night distinction; 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 applies day and night below 10,000 ft MSL.

5. Ceiling constraint — § 91.155(c): apart from Special VFR (§ 91.157), no VFR flight beneath the ceiling within the lateral boundaries of controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport when the ceiling is below 1,000 ft. This bites on surface-area Class E even when visibility and cloud clearance are otherwise satisfied.

6. Surface-area Class E is not a separate weather-minimum row; it uses the same 'less than 10,000 ft MSL' figures, but adds the § 91.155(c) ceiling restriction and the § 91.155(d) ground-visibility requirement for takeoff/landing/traffic-pattern operations.

7. Adjacent but out of scope here: Special VFR (§ 91.157); the Class G exceptions in § 91.155(b); the Class B/C/D rows (3 SM, clear of clouds for B; 3 SM, 500/1,000/2,000 for C and D); student-pilot limitations in § 61.89(a)(6)-(7).

QUICK-REFERENCE TABLE (14 CFR § 91.155(a))

  Class E, < 10,000 ft MSL : 3 SM : 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal
  Class E, >= 10,000 ft MSL: 5 SM : 1,000 below / 1,000 above / 1 SM horizontal

JURISDICTION AND VERSION NOTE

Figures above are U.S. FAA rules (14 CFR Part 91) as currently published in the eCFR, fetched 2026-11-15. Other ICAO states set different Class E minimums (commonly 5 km visibility and 1,500 m horizontal / 300 m vertical / 300 m above), so the answer must not be exported to a non-FAA jurisdiction without re-checking that state's AIP or regulations.

answer:
OSHA PERMISSIBLE EXPOSURE LIMIT AND ACTION LEVEL — RESPIRABLE CRYSTALLINE SILICA, GENERAL INDUSTRY

1. ANSWER

  Quantity            Value                 Unit / basis                         Regulatory source
  ------------------  --------------------  -----------------------------------  -------------------------------
  PEL                 50                    µg/m³, 8-hour TWA                   29 CFR 1910.1053(c)
  Action level        25                    µg/m³, 8-hour TWA                   29 CFR 1910.1053(b) (definition)

  Unit conversions: 50 µg/m³ = 0.050 mg/m³; 25 µg/m³ = 0.025 mg/m³.
  The action level is exactly one-half the PEL.

  Both figures are for TOTAL respirable crystalline silica — quartz, cristobalite and/or tridymite taken together. 29 CFR 1910.1053 does not set separate polymorph-specific limits.

2. VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT (as fetched 2026-11-15)

  Paragraph (c) Permissible exposure limit (PEL):
    "The employer shall ensure that no employee is exposed to an airborne concentration of respirable crystalline silica in excess of 50 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."
    — eCFR, 29 CFR 1910.1053, sha256 0eac440a5987; corroborated by CFR 2023 title 29 vol 6 PDF, sha256 95d20be78ec2.

  Paragraph (b) Definitions — Action level:
    "Action level means a concentration of airborne respirable crystalline silica of 25 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA."
    — same sources.

  Paragraph (b) Definitions — Respirable crystalline silica:
    "quartz, cristobalite, and/or tridymite contained in airborne particles that are determined to be respirable by a sampling device designed to meet the characteristics for respirable-particle-size-selective samplers specified in ISO 7708:1995."

  Paragraph (b) Definitions — Employee exposure:
    "the exposure to airborne respirable crystalline silica that would occur if the employee were not using a respirator."

3. HOW THE NUMBERS ARE MEASURED / APPLIED

  - Metric: 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA) airborne concentration of the respirable particle-size fraction, sampled with an ISO 7708:1995-conforming respirable sampler (e.g., cyclone + filter, or a size-selective sampler meeting that convention).
  - Exposure is determined WITHOUT credit for respirator use (paragraph (b), 'employee exposure'). Respirators reduce the employee's actual intake and are used to supplement controls, but do not change the measured exposure value used against the PEL and action level.
  - The PEL is a ceiling on the 8-hour TWA: compliance means the 8-hour TWA is not in excess of 50 µg/m³. A result of exactly 50 µg/m³ is AT the PEL, not above it; 'above the PEL' means >50.
  - The action level is a trigger, not a separate enforceable exposure limit: exposures at or above 25 µg/m³ (≥25) activate exposure-assessment and program obligations; below 25 µg/m³ the employee falls outside the assessment requirement of paragraph (d)(1).

4. WHAT EACH NUMBER TRIGGERS (for context; the request asked only for the two figures)

  At or above the action level (≥25 µg/m³, 8-hr TWA):
    - Exposure assessment required for each employee who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed at or above the action level (paragraph (d)(1)).
    - Repeat monitoring at least every 6 months while exposures remain at or above the AL but at or below the PEL (paragraph (d)(3)(iii)).
    - Medical surveillance offered to employees exposed at or above the AL for 30 or more days per year (paragraph (i)(1)). NOTE: paragraph (i) was not in the fetched excerpts; verify the 30-day trigger against the current text before relying on it for program design.

  Above the PEL (>50 µg/m³, 8-hr TWA):
    - Engineering and work-practice controls required to reduce and maintain exposure to or below the PEL unless infeasible; if infeasible, controls to the lowest feasible level plus respiratory protection (paragraph (f)(1)).
    - Repeat monitoring within 3 months of the most recent monitoring (paragraph (d)(3)(iv)).

  Regardless of measured level:
    - Written exposure control plan with task inventory, controls per task, and housekeeping measures (paragraph (f)(2)).

5. SCOPE AND CAVEATS

  - General industry = 29 CFR 1910.1053. Construction has its own standard, 29 CFR 1926.1153, which carries the same 50 µg/m³ PEL and 25 µg/m³ action level (Table 1 is a task-based compliance alternative). Shipyard/maritime employment is addressed in 29 CFR 1915.1053. If the workplace task is indistinguishable from a 1926.1153 Table 1 construction task and is not performed regularly in the same environment, 1910.1053 does not apply (paragraph (a)(3), quoted in the fetched text).
  - Federal OSHA is the baseline. State-plan states must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may adopt a lower PEL or lower action level; a state plan may also have a different compliance date history. Confirm the applicable state plan's silica rule before finalizing exposure limits for a facility in a state-plan jurisdiction.
  - Currency: the 50 / 25 µg/m³ values were confirmed against the 2023 printed CFR and against the current eCFR text fetched 2026-11-15. The silica rule took effect June 23, 2016; general-industry engineering-controls compliance began June 23, 2018. The pre-2016 formula-based PEL for quartz (10 mg/m³ divided by %SiO2 + 2, with related cristobalite/tridymite formulas) is SUPERSEDED for general industry and must not be used.
  - No short-term exposure limit: 1910.1053 sets a single 8-hour TWA PEL and does not establish a separate STEL or excursion limit. (Verify against the current full text; paragraph (c) as fetched contains only the 8-hour TWA limit.)
  - For comparison only, not law: ACGIH TLV-TWA = 25 µg/m³ (respirable quartz); NIOSH REL = 50 µg/m³ (8-hr TWA). These are advisory and numerically coincide with the AL and PEL respectively.

6. FIVE-MINUTE VERIFICATION PROCEDURE

  a. Open eCFR: ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/section-1910.1053.
  b. Confirm paragraph (c) reads 'in excess of 50 µg/m3, calculated as an 8-hour TWA'.

answer:
ANSWER

The 1876 pocket manual requires a TWO-THIRDS VOTE to adopt a motion for the Previous Question (i.e., to carry the question 'Shall the main question be now put?').

SOURCE OF RECORD

Henry M. Robert, *Robert's Rules of Order: Pocket Manual of Rules of Order for Deliberative Assemblies* (1876), Project Gutenberg eBook No. 9097.
- Plain text: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/9097/9097-0.txt
- HTML: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/9097/pg9097-images.html
- Catalog record (confirms 1876 first publication and the 'Pocket Manual' title): https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/9097

VERBATIM PASSAGE (the operative statement)

"...only necessary for some one to obtain the floor and 'call for the previous question;' this call being seconded, the chairman, as it allows of no debate, instantly puts the question, thus: 'Shall the main question be now put?' If this is carried by a two-thirds vote [§ 68], all debate instantly ceases, excepting that the member who offered the original resolution, or reported it from a committee, is, as in all other cases, entitled to the floor to close the debate; after which, the chairman immediately puts the questions to the assembly, first, on the motion to commit, if it is pending; if this is carried, of course the subject goes to the committee; if, however, it fails, the vote is next taken on amendments, and finally on the resolution as amended."

CORROBORATION WITHIN THE SAME TEXT

Section 68 of the manual is headed: "68. Motions requiring a two-thirds vote.* [See Two-thirds Vote, page 159, and § 39 of Rules of Order.]" — the Previous Question is one of the motions in that class, and the cross-reference in the passage above ("[§ 68]") is the manual's own pointer to it. The two statements agree: the Previous Question is adopted by a two-thirds vote.

PROCEDURE AS THE 1876 TEXT DESCRIBES IT (for completeness)

1. A member obtains the floor and 'calls for the previous question.'
2. The call must be seconded (a procedural prerequisite, not part of the vote threshold).
3. Because the motion allows of no debate, the chair instantly puts the question: 'Shall the main question be now put?'
4. If carried by a two-thirds vote, all debate instantly ceases, except that the member who offered the original resolution (or reported it from a committee) is entitled to the floor to close debate.
5. The chair then puts the pending questions in order: first the motion to commit (if pending); if that fails, then amendments; finally the resolution as amended.
6. If the call fails (i.e., debate is not cut off), debate continues as if the motion had not been made.
7. If a motion to postpone (definitely or indefinitely), a motion to reconsider, or an appeal is pending, the previous question is exhausted by the vote on that motion and does not cut off debate on other pending motions.

THREE THINGS THAT MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH THIS ANSWER

(a) The sentence elsewhere in the manual — "If an assembly has adopted no Rules of Order, then a majority vote is sufficient for the adoption of any motion, except to 'suspend the rules,' which would require a unanimous vote" — states the default for bodies that have adopted NO rules of order. It does not govern a body operating under the manual, and it does not lower the Previous Question threshold for such a body. It is not a competing answer.
(b) The 'Forms of Putting Certain Questions' section ('If the Previous Question is demanded, it is put thus: "Shall the main question be now put?"') prescribes wording only; it states no threshold and neither confirms nor contradicts the two-thirds requirement.
(c) Project Gutenberg eBook No. 75990 is the 1915 *Rules of Order Revised*, a different edition, and its quoted congressional rule ('a motion for the previous question, which, being ordered by a majority of members voting, if a quorum be present...') is a reproduction of U.S. House rules inside that later edition, not the manual's own requirement. It is excluded from this answer. The answer above is drawn solely from the 1876 text (No. 9097).

SCOPE AND LIMITS OF WHAT WAS VERIFIED

The threshold itself — two-thirds — is stated explicitly and unambiguously in the 1876 text, so no interpretive convention is needed to reach it. What the retrieved passages do NOT spell out is the base of the fraction (two-thirds of the votes cast versus two-thirds of the members present): the manual says only 'a two-thirds vote' and footnotes its general 'Two-thirds Vote' discussion at page 159, which was not retrieved here. If a downstream user needs that base, it should be read from page 159 of the 1876 edition (and § 39 of the Rules of Order) rather than assumed. The adoption threshold itself is not in doubt.

question: H15
answer:
## Classification of a 65 °C flash-point liquid under the US HMR (49 CFR)

### 1. Answer
**No. It is not a Class 3 flammable liquid.** On the stated facts — a flash point of 65 °C and no other hazard class — the liquid meets the HMR definition of a **combustible liquid** in 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1).

### 2. Basis in the regulation
49 CFR 173.120(a) defines a flammable liquid (Class 3) as:

> “a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging…”

A 65 °C flash point is above 60 °C, so the liquid does not meet the first branch of the Class 3 definition. Nothing in the facts says the material is intentionally heated and offered for transport at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, so the elevated-temperature branch is not triggered.

49 CFR 173.120(b)(1) defines a combustible liquid as:

> “any liquid that does not meet the definition of any other hazard class specified in this subchapter and has a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F).”

The stated flash point of 65 °C is above 60 °C and below 93 °C, and the facts state that the liquid meets no other hazard class. It is therefore a combustible liquid.

### 3. Measurement-method condition
49 CFR 173.120(c) defines flash point by specified closed-cup test procedures, such as ASTM D 56, D 3278, or D 3828 for certain low-viscosity liquids, and ASTM D 93 for other liquids. The “No” answer assumes that the 65 °C figure is a closed-cup flash point determined under 173.120(c). If 65 °C is an open-cup value, it cannot be used directly for classification; the material must be tested by an authorized closed-cup method. Because open-cup results are generally higher than closed-cup results, an open-cup 65 °C could correspond to a closed-cup value at or below 60 °C, which would make the material Class 3. If the method is unknown, the classification is conditional until a 173.120(c) flash point is available.

### 4. Regulatory consequences of being a combustible liquid
Being a combustible liquid is not the same as being unregulated in every case. Applicability depends on packaging and on whether the material is a hazardous substance, hazardous waste, or marine pollutant:

- **Non-bulk packaging:** Under 173.150(f)(2), the HMR do not apply to a material classed as a combustible liquid in a non-bulk packaging unless the material is a hazardous substance, a hazardous waste, or a marine pollutant.
- **Bulk packaging, or hazardous substance/hazardous waste/marine pollutant:** Under 173.150(f)(3), the material is not subject to all HMR requirements, but remains subject to the requirements enumerated there, which include shipping papers, waybills, switching orders and hazardous waste manifests; marking of packages; display of identification numbers on bulk packages; placarding for bulk packagings; carriage aboard aircraft and vessels; emergency response information; and registration for bulk packagings.
- **Shipping description:** Under 172.101(d)(4), Class 3 entries in the Hazardous Materials Table are modified to read “Combustible liquid” when the material has a flash point above 60 °C but below 93 °C. If a shipping description is required, the applicable Class 3 entry is used with “Combustible liquid” in place of the Class 3 designation, not as a Class 3 flammable liquid. PHMSA’s interpretation for pine oil with a closed-cup flash point of 75 °C illustrates the same result: “UN1272, Pine oil, Combustible liquid, PG III,” not “UN1272, Pine oil, 3, PG III.”
- **Non-sustaining combustion:** Under 173.120(b)(3), a combustible liquid that does not sustain combustion is not subject to the HMR as a combustible liquid. Either ASTM D 4206 or appendix H of part 173 may be used to make that determination.
- **Elevated temperature:** If the liquid is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its 65 °C flash point in a bulk packaging, it would meet the elevated-temperature branch of the Class 3 definition in 173.120(a) and would be Class 3 notwithstanding the 65 °C flash point. That fact is not stated here.
- **Vessel/aircraft:** The domestic combustible-liquid treatment is a US HMR concept. International modal rules such as IMDG and IATA do not use the same combustible-liquid category; a liquid with a flash point above 60 °C is generally not Class 3 there, though it may be regulated if it is a marine pollutant or environmentally hazardous substance. This does not change the US domestic answer.

### 5. Bottom line
For US domestic transport under the HMR, a liquid with a closed-cup flash point of 65 °C that meets no other hazard class is **not a Class 3 flammable liquid**. It is a **combustible liquid** under 49 CFR 173.120(b)(1). Whether any HMR requirements actually apply depends on whether it is in bulk or non-bulk packaging and whether it is a hazardous substance, hazardous waste, or marine pollutant; non-bulk shipments are generally not regulated unless one of those conditions applies.

question: H17
answer:
NRC DOSE LIMITS FOR INDIVIDUAL MEMBERS OF THE PUBLIC FROM A LICENSEE'S OPERATIONS

Source: 10 CFR Part 20, Subpart D (Radiation Dose Limits for Individual Members of the Public), principally 10 CFR 20.1301, with the compliance-demonstration provisions of 10 CFR 20.1302 and the definitions in 10 CFR 20.1003. Text as currently published on eCFR (verified against ecfr.gov pages for 20.1301, Subpart D, and 20.1003).

=====================================================================
1. THE TWO LIMITS, STATED DIRECTLY
=====================================================================

ANNUAL LIMIT - 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(1)
  0.1 rem (1 mSv) total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) per year,
  to individual members of the public, from the licensed operation.
  Equivalents: 0.1 rem = 100 mrem = 1 mSv = 1,000 microsievert.

HOURLY LIMIT IN AN UNRESTRICTED AREA - 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(2)
  0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in any one hour,
  the dose in any unrestricted area from external sources.
  Equivalents: 0.002 rem = 2 mrem = 0.02 mSv = 20 microsievert per hour.

Both are obligations on the licensee: 'Each licensee shall conduct operations so that--' the two conditions in (a)(1) and (a)(2) are met. They are concurrent requirements, not alternatives; a licensee must satisfy both.

=====================================================================
2. VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT (10 CFR 20.1301(a))
=====================================================================

'(a) Each licensee shall conduct operations so that--

(1) The total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year, exclusive of the dose contributions from background radiation, from any medical administration the individual has received, from exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under Sec. 35.75, from voluntary participation in medical research programs, and from the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with Sec. 20.2003, and

(2) The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources, exclusive of the dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with Sec. 35.75, does not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 millisievert) in any one hour.'

[56 FR 23398, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 48625 (Sept. 20, 1995); 62 FR 4133 (Jan. 29, 1997); 67 FR 20370 (Apr. 24, 2002); 67 FR 62872 (Oct. 9, 2002)]

=====================================================================
3. WHAT EACH LIMIT COVERS (SCOPE)
=====================================================================

Annual limit, 20.1301(a)(1):
  - Quantity: total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) - i.e., the sum of external effective dose equivalent plus committed effective dose equivalent from intakes. It is a whole-body-effective quantity, not a single-organ or skin-only quantity.
  - Source: 'from the licensed operation' - all pathways from the licensed operation (direct radiation, airborne and liquid effluent, and other releases), not direct radiation alone.
  - Excluded from the 0.1 rem: background radiation; medical administration the individual has received; exposure to patients administered radioactive material and released under 10 CFR 35.75; voluntary participation in medical research programs; and the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage under 20.2003.

Hourly limit, 20.1301(a)(2):
  - Quantity: dose from EXTERNAL SOURCES only (no inhalation/ingestion component). It is a dose-rate ceiling on external radiation levels in unrestricted areas.
  - Location: 'in any unrestricted area' - i.e., measured/assessed where members of the public may be, not inside a restricted area.
  - Only exclusion: dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released under 35.75.
  - Not a permissible sustained rate (see Section 6).

=====================================================================
4. OPERATIVE DEFINITIONS (10 CFR 20.1003 and 20.1003-adjacent)
=====================================================================

Unrestricted area - an area to which access is neither limited nor controlled by the licensee (contrast: 'controlled area' = an area outside a restricted area but inside the site boundary, access to which can be limited by the licensee for any reason; 'restricted area' = an area to which access is limited by the licensee for purposes of protection of individuals against undue risks from exposure to radiation and radioactive materials).

Member of the public - an individual except when that individual is receiving an occupational dose (i.e., a person who is not a radiation worker for the licensee).

Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) - the sum of the deep-dose equivalent (external whole-body) and the committed effective dose equivalent from internal intakes.

Committed effective dose equivalent (HE,50) - the sum over irradiated organs/tissues of wT x HT,50, where HT,50 is the committed dose equivalent to tissue T over the 50-year period following intake.

Site boundary - the line beyond which land or property is not owned, leased, or otherwise controlled by the licensee.

Note on controlled-area access: 20.1301(b) - if the licensee permits members of the public to have access to controlled areas, the public limits continue to apply to those individuals.

=====================================================================
5. RELATED AND ADJACENT FIGURES IN SUBPART D (for completeness; none replaces the two limits above)
=====================================================================

| Provision        | Figure                          | Applies to                                                                 |
|------------------|---------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 20.1301(a)(1)    | 0.1 rem (1 mSv) per year        | TEDE to individual members of the public from the licensed operation       |
| 20.1301(a)(2)    | 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) per hour   | External-source dose in any unrestricted area                              |
| 20.1301(c)       | 0.5 rem (5 mSv)                 | Visitor dose to a patient who cannot be released under 35.75, with prior authorized-user determination |
| 20.1301(d)       | 0.5 rem (5 mSv) per year        | Only on prior NRC authorization; applicant must show need/duration, an assessment-and-control program, and ALARA procedures |
| 20.1302(b)(2)(ii)| 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) per hour AND 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) per year | External-source dose if an individual were continuously present in an unrestricted area - used when demonstrating compliance via the effluent-concentration path |
| 20.1301(e)       | 40 CFR Part 190                 | Licensees subject to EPA generally applicable environmental radiation standards must also comply with them |
| 20.1301(f)       | Additional restrictions      | Commission may impose further limits on unrestricted-area levels and effluent quantities to restrict collective dose |

Unit check across the table: 0.1 rem = 1 mSv; 0.002 rem = 0.02 mSv; 0.5 rem = 5 mSv; 0.05 rem = 0.5 mSv. All conversions use 1 rem = 10 mSv.

=====================================================================
6. WHY THE HOURLY FIGURE IS NOT AN ANNUAL RATE
=====================================================================

The hourly limit is a short-term ceiling on external dose rate, not a rate that may be sustained. 0.002 rem/h held continuously for a year would be 0.002 x 8,760 = 17.52 rem, which is 175 times the 0.1 rem annual limit. The regulations close this gap in two ways:
  (a) 20.1301(a)(1) independently caps annual TEDE at 0.1 rem regardless of short-term rates; and
  (b) where the licensee demonstrates compliance through 20.1302(b)(2), the criterion is that, if an individual were continuously present in an unrestricted area, external-source dose would not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in an hour AND 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) in a year. The 0.05 rem/y figure, spread over 8,760 hours, corresponds to an average of about 5.7 microrem/h (approx. 0.057 microsievert/h) - roughly 350 times below the hourly ceiling. Practically, the annual criterion binds for continuous occupancy; the hourly criterion binds for transient, high-rate situations (e.g., a temporary source movement or a shielded-storage configuration change).

=====================================================================
7. HOW COMPLIANCE IS DEMONSTRATED (10 CFR 20.1302)
=====================================================================

20.1302(a): the licensee must make, or cause to be made, surveys of radiation levels in unrestricted and controlled areas and of radioactive material in effluents released to those areas, sufficient to demonstrate compliance with the 20.1301 limits.

20.1302(b): the licensee shows compliance with the annual limit by EITHER
  (1) demonstrating by measurement or calculation that the TEDE to the individual likely to receive the highest dose from the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem/y; OR
  (2) demonstrating that (i) annual average concentrations of radioactive material in gaseous and liquid effluents at the unrestricted-area boundary do not exceed Table 2 of Appendix B to Part 20, AND (ii) if an individual were continuously present in an unrestricted area, external-source dose would not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in an hour and 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) in a year.

=====================================================================
8. CAVEATS A USER SHOULD KNOW
=====================================================================

1. These are the NRC federal limits in 10 CFR Part 20. Agreement States adopt compatible regulations under their own citations; the numbering and occasionally the wording differ, though the numerical values are required to be compatible. Facility-specific license conditions, NRC orders, or 20.1301(d) authorizations can be more restrictive or, for (d), less restrictive than 0.1 rem/y.
2. 20.1301(e) preserves EPA's 40 CFR Part 190 standards for licensees subject to them (uranium fuel cycle operations); where both apply, the more restrictive governs in practice.
3. The values above are current as published on eCFR at the time of retrieval and reflect the section as last amended in 2002 (67 FR 62872). Historical versions of Part 20 (pre-1991) used different quantities and values and are not reflected here.
4. The 0.1 rem/y figure is TEDE and thus already aggregates internal and external dose; do not add effluent-derived internal dose on top of it as a separate allowance.

=====================================================================
9. DIRECT ANSWER, CONDENSED
=====================================================================

Per year: 0.1 rem (1 mSv) total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from the licensed operation - 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(1).

In any one hour in an unrestricted area: 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) from external sources - 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(2).

COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — FMCSA ALCOHOL CONCENTRATION THRESHOLD

Answer: 0.04 or greater. A driver subject to 49 CFR Part 382 may not report for duty or remain on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. The threshold is inclusive; a result of exactly 0.04 is prohibited. The regulatory unit is grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath (g/210 L breath) as indicated by an evidential breath test under Part 40; this is equivalent to 0.04% BAC for communication purposes.

Authority: 49 CFR 382.201 provides: 'No driver shall report for duty or remain on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. No employer having knowledge that a driver has an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater shall permit the driver to perform or continue to perform safety-sensitive functions.' 49 CFR 382.107 defines 'alcohol concentration (or content)' as 'the alcohol in a volume of breath expressed in terms of grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath as indicated by an evidential breath test under this part.'

What the threshold covers: 'Safety-sensitive function' is defined in §382.107 to include all time from when a driver begins work or is required to be in readiness to work until relieved, including waiting to be dispatched, inspecting/servicing equipment, driving, loading/unloading, and attending a disabled vehicle. The prohibition is therefore not limited to driving time.

Other alcohol prohibitions that do not depend on reaching 0.04: §382.205 prohibits any use of alcohol while performing safety-sensitive functions; §382.207 prohibits performing safety-sensitive functions within four hours after using alcohol; §382.209 prohibits a driver required to take a post-accident alcohol test from using alcohol for eight hours following the accident or until the test, whichever occurs first. Thus, a driver can be barred from safety-sensitive duty for alcohol use at a concentration below 0.04 if the conduct violates those provisions. The concentration-based bar is 0.04.

Testing levels: Under 49 CFR 40.245, a screening test result of 0.02 or greater requires a confirmation test. A confirmation result of 0.02 through 0.039 is below the §382.201 prohibition but is addressed as 'other alcohol-related conduct' under §382.505; the driver must not perform safety-sensitive functions for 24 hours. A confirmation result of 0.04 or greater is a violation of §382.201.

Consequences at 0.04 or greater: The driver must be removed from safety-sensitive functions, including driving, and the employer must not permit the driver to perform them (§382.501). Before return, the driver must complete the DOT return-to-duty process: evaluation by a substance abuse professional, completion of education/treatment, a return-to-duty alcohol test with a result less than 0.02, and follow-up testing (§§382.503, 382.605, 382.309, 382.311). An alcohol confirmation test result of 0.04 or higher is reportable to the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse under Part 382 Subpart G.

Not the 0.08 limit: 0.08% is the common state criminal per se DUI threshold, not the FMCSA safety-sensitive threshold. The federal CMV rule uses 0.04. State CDL disqualification and criminal BAC limits are outside this determination.

Result: value 0.04; unit g/210 L breath (equivalent to 0.04% BAC).

answer:
STATUTORY PAID ANNUAL LEAVE — GREAT BRITAIN (ENGLAND, SCOTLAND AND WALES)

ANSWERS
1. Weekly entitlement: 5.6 weeks of paid annual leave per leave year.
2. Cap: 28 days.

LEGAL BASIS
- Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), as amended, which extend to England, Scotland and Wales (E+W+S). Northern Ireland has its own Working Time Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1998; the figures are the same in practice, but the GB instrument is the authority for this answer.
- Regulation 13(1): 4 weeks' annual leave in each leave year (the EU-derived 'basic' 4 weeks).
- Regulation 13A(1) and 13A(2)(e): a further 1.6 weeks of 'additional' annual leave in any leave year beginning on or after 1 April 2009.
- Aggregate: 4 weeks + 1.6 weeks = 5.6 weeks.
- Regulation 13A(3): 'The aggregate entitlement provided for in paragraph (2) and regulation 13(1) is subject to a maximum of 28 days.' That is the 28-day cap.
- Consistent with GOV.UK ('almost all people classed as workers are legally entitled to 5.6 weeks' paid holiday a year'; 'Statutory paid holiday entitlement is limited to 28 days') and Acas ('By law, workers are entitled to 5.6 weeks' statutory paid holiday a year'; 'Statutory paid holiday is limited to 28 days').

HOW THE TWO FIGURES FIT TOGETHER
The 28-day cap is the same entitlement as 5.6 weeks expressed in days for a worker who works 5 days a week:

    5.6 weeks × 5 working days per week = 28 days

So for the standard full-time 5-day-week worker the two answers coincide: 5.6 weeks = 28 days, and the worker is exactly at the cap. The cap is not an extra 28 days on top of the 5.6 weeks; it is the ceiling on the combined 4 weeks + 1.6 weeks.

CALCULATION RULE (GOV.UK 'Calculating holiday entitlement' method)
Statutory leave in days for a worker with a full leave year is the lower of:
(a) 28 days; or
(b) 5.6 × days worked per week.

Worked examples (each checked against the 28-day cap):
- 5 days/week: 5.6 × 5 = 28.0 days → 28 days (at the cap).
- 4 days/week: 5.6 × 4 = 22.4 days → 22.4 days (below the cap).
- 3 days/week: 5.6 × 3 = 16.8 days → 16.8 days (below the cap).
- 6 days/week: 5.6 × 6 = 33.6 days, but the cap applies → 28 days.
- Compressed hours (fixed weekly hours, unequal days): calculate entitlement in days using the rule above, then multiply by the average length of the working day to express it in hours.
- Shift workers: the lower of 5.6 weeks × average shifts per week, or 28 days' worth of shifts, where average shifts per week = (shifts per shift pattern ÷ calendar days per shift pattern) × 7.

WHO IS COVERED
'Worker' is used in the statutory sense. The 5.6 weeks applies to employees and to other workers, including agency workers, zero-hours workers, workers with irregular hours, and part-year workers. Entitlement accrues from the first day of work, including during a probationary period.

PART-TIME, IRREGULAR-HOURS AND PART-YEAR WORKERS
- Part-time workers with regular hours: 5.6 weeks, pro-rated by days worked per week (fewer than 28 days, as in the examples above).
- Irregular-hours workers and part-year workers: entitlement is 5.6 weeks, but for leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024 it accrues on the basis of hours actually worked, using the statutory 12.07% accrual rate (regs 15B–15C), with special rules for accrual during sick leave and statutory leave. 12.07% is an accrual rate, not a different weekly entitlement: 52 weeks − 5.6 weeks = 46.4 weeks, and 5.6 ÷ 46.4 = 12.07%.
- Workers who join or leave mid-year receive a proportion of the 5.6 weeks equal to the proportion of the leave year worked.

BANK HOLIDAYS
Bank and public holidays do not have to be given as paid leave, and an employer may include them within the 5.6 weeks / 28 days. If bank holidays are included, the worker still receives no less than 5.6 weeks in total; if the employer gives them in addition, that is a contractual enhancement above the statutory floor.

STATUTORY FLOOR, NOT A TYPICAL ENTITLEMENT
The 5.6 weeks / 28 days is a minimum. An employer may contractually offer more; any extra leave is not subject to all the statutory rules (for example, a qualifying period may apply to it).

CARRY-OVER AND PAYMENT IN LIEU (context for applying the figures)
- The 4 weeks under reg 13 cannot be replaced by a payment in lieu except on termination of employment.
- The 1.6 weeks under reg 13A may be carried forward into the following leave year by a relevant agreement, and may be paid in lieu only in the limited circumstances set out in reg 13A(6).
- Carry-over of the 4 weeks is required where the worker could not take leave because of sickness or family-related leave (subject to the limits established by case law).

SOURCES FOR VERIFICATION
- Working Time Regulations 1998, regs 13 and 13A (in particular reg 13A(2)(e) and reg 13A(3)), legislation.gov.uk.
- GOV.UK, 'Holiday entitlement: Entitlement' (5.6 weeks; 28-day limit; bank holidays may be included).
- GOV.UK, 'How to calculate holiday entitlement for workers on different types of contract' (lower of 28 days or 5.6 × days worked per week).
- Acas, 'Holiday entitlement' (5.6 weeks; limited to 28 days).

From the original DNS specification, RFC 1035 §2.3.4 'Size limits':

- Label: maximum 63 octets of label content. The 63-octet limit is the label data itself; the wire-format length octet that precedes each label is not counted as part of the 63. This follows from the 6-bit length field in RFC 1035 §3.1, which can represent values 0–63.
- Full domain name: maximum 255 octets in wire-format encoding. This count includes every label length octet and the terminating zero-length root label. In textual presentation the name is shorter: at most 253 characters excluding the trailing dot, or 254 including the trailing dot, because presentation format omits the length octets and the root terminator.

The 512-octet UDP message limit also listed in RFC 1035 §2.3.4 is a transport/packet limit, not the domain-name or label limit; it does not change the 63-octet label bound or the 255-octet wire-format name bound.

Answer: label = 63 octets; full domain name = 255 octets (wire-encoded, including length octets and root label).

answer:
US FEDERAL MAXIMUM CONTAMINANT LEVEL (MCL) FOR PFOA IN DRINKING WATER

ANSWER
  MCL = 4.0 nanograms per litre (ng/L) = 4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) = 0.0000040 mg/L.
  This is the enforceable individual MCL for perfluorooctanoic acid under the EPA's 2024 PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (NPDWR), 40 CFR Part 141, Subpart Z (89 FR 32750, Apr. 26, 2024).

1. AS THE RULE LISTS IT — CODIFIED TEXT
   40 CFR 141.61(c), Table 1 to Paragraph (c), "MCLs and HBWCs for PFAS", row (vi):

     CAS No.        Contaminant   MCL (mg/l) (unless otherwise noted)   HBWC (mg/l) for Hazard Index calculation
     (vi) 45285-51-6   PFOA        0.0000040                              Not applicable.

   So the codified, enforceable number is 0.0000040 mg/L. The table's column heading is "mg/l (unless otherwise noted)"; the same table's footnote and the companion HI equation use ng/L for the PFAS concentrations, and the preamble (below) states the ng/L form explicitly.

2. AS THE RULE LISTS IT — FEDERAL REGISTER PREAMBLE (89 FR 32750, Apr. 26, 2024)
   "Through this action, the EPA is finalizing MCLGs for PFOA and PFOS at zero. Considering feasibility, the EPA is promulgating individual Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for PFOA and PFOS at 4.0 nanograms per liter (ng/L) or parts per trillion (ppt)."

   And, in the rule summary:
   "The EPA is finalizing MCLGs for PFOA and PFOS at zero (0) and enforceable MCLs for PFOA and PFOS at 4.0 ng/L (ng/L or ppt)."

3. AS EPA'S REGULATORY SUMMARY LISTS IT
   PFOA: Final MCLG = Zero; Final MCL (enforceable) = "4.0 parts per trillion (ppt) (also expressed as ng/L)".

4. IN NANograms PER LITRE — THE CONVERSION, SHOWN IN FULL
   The rule already states the ng/L figure, so this is a unit restatement, not an independent calculation. Both directions:

   (a) From the codified mg/L value:
       0.0000040 mg/L x (1,000,000 ng / 1 mg) = 4.0 ng/L
       (mg/L -> ng/L factor is 10^6; 4.0 x 10^-6 mg/L = 4.0 x 10^0 ng/L.)

   (b) From ppt:
       1 ppt = 1 part per 10^12 = 1 ng per kg of water; at unit density (1 kg/L) this is 1 ng/L. EPA uses 1 ppt = 1 ng/L for drinking water.
       Therefore 4.0 ppt = 4.0 ng/L.

   Result: 4.0 ng/L, exactly, to the two significant figures the rule uses. No rounding decision is required and none is made.

5. VALUES THAT ARE NOT THE PFOA MCL — DO NOT SUBSTITUTE THESE
   - MCLG (Maximum Contaminant Level Goal) for PFOA = zero (0). Non-enforceable health goal; the enforceable MCL is 4.0 ng/L. The rule sets both, and they differ.
   - PFOA monitoring TRIGGER LEVEL = 2.0 ng/L (40 CFR 141.902(a)(5), Table 1 to Paragraph (a)(5)). This is a monitoring/reporting trigger for reduced monitoring, not the MCL. It is exactly one-half of the 4.0 ng/L MCL, so the two are internally consistent, but they must not be interchanged.
   - Hazard Index (HI) MCL = 1 (unitless). The HI applies to mixtures containing two or more of PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA and PFBS. PFOA is NOT an HI component and has no HBWC (table entry: "Not applicable"). The HI value of 1 does not apply to PFOA.
   - Companion individual MCLs, for contrast only: PFOS 4.0 ng/L (0.0000040 mg/L); PFHxS 10 ng/L; PFNA 10 ng/L; HFPO-DA 10 ng/L (each 0.00001 mg/L); PFBS has no individual MCL (HBWC 2000 ng/L for HI purposes only).

6. COMPLIANCE CONTEXT (what the 4.0 ng/L number means operationally)
   - Rule effective date: June 25, 2024 (FR DATES line).
   - MCL compliance deadline: April 26, 2029 (40 CFR 141.900(b)(4)) — as the eCFR text stood at retrieval.
   - Initial monitoring results reported to the State by April 26, 2027; compliance monitoring requirements met by April 26, 2027; analytical requirements by June 25, 2024 (§141.900(b)).
   - Compliance is judged on a running annual average at each sampling point, not on a single sample (§§141.903, 141.905). A single result more than 4x the MCL is treated as an MCL violation in the reporting rules (§141.904).
   - Applies to community water systems and non-transient, non-community water systems (§141.900(a)).
   - Best available technologies identified for PFOA: anion exchange, GAC, reverse osmosis, nanofiltration (40 CFR 141.61(d), Table 3).

7. VERIFICATION / STATUS NOTE
   The figure above is taken from the codified text of 40 CFR 141.61(c) and the Federal Register preamble of the final PFAS NPDWR as retrieved (eCFR Title 40, Part 141, Subpart Z, and §141.61; govinfo FR-2024-04-26 / 2024-07773; EPA SDWA PFAS page). At retrieval the codified entry still read 0.0000040 mg/L for PFOA and Subpart Z remained in force. Before relying on this for a compliance determination, re-check the current eCFR text of §141.61(c) and §141.900(b) for: (i) any amendment to the MCL itself, (ii) any change to the April 26, 2029 compliance deadline (extensions have been under consideration), and (iii) the effect of any court action on Subpart Z. Any such change would alter the compliance date or the surrounding framework, not the 4.0 ng/L (0.0000040 mg/L) codified value as of this answer.

8. ONE-LINE CITABLE STATEMENT
   "The US federal MCL for PFOA is 4.0 ng/L (4.0 ppt), codified at 40 CFR 141.61(c) as 0.0000040 mg/L, promulgated in the PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation, 89 FR 32750 (Apr. 26, 2024), effective June 25, 2024, with MCL compliance required by April 26, 2029."

# IANA HTTP Status Code Registry — Entry 425

## Answers

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| Name (Description) of status code 425 | **Too Early** |
| RFC reference for status code 425 | **RFC 8470** |

Full entry as registered: `425 — Too Early — [RFC 8470]`

## Evidence 1 — IANA registry, CSV format (authoritative, machine-readable)

Source: <https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-status-codes/http-status-codes-1.csv> (registry last updated 2025-09-15).

Row 425 in context, quoted verbatim from the CSV (surrounding rows included to fix the position unambiguously):

```csv
423,Locked,[RFC 4918]
424,Failed Dependency,[RFC 4918]
425,Too Early,[RFC 8470]
426,Upgrade Required,"[RFC 9110, Section 15.5.22]"
```

Column order is declared by the CSV header as `Value,Description,Reference`. Therefore for value `425`: Description = `Too Early`, Reference = `[RFC 8470]`.

## Evidence 2 — IANA registry, HTML format

Source: <https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-status-codes> (Last Updated 2025-09-15).

The HTML table renders the same three cells:

```
Value   Description   Reference
...
424     Failed Dependency   RFC 4918
425     Too Early           RFC 8470
426     Upgrade Required   RFC 9110, Section 15.5.22
...
```

## Evidence 3 — IANA registry, XML format

Source: <https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-status-codes/http-status-codes.xml>.

The XML record sequence lists `425` immediately followed by the description `Too Early`, in the same position between `424 / Failed Dependency` and `426 / Upgrade Required`, i.e. no code is skipped or renumbered relative to the CSV and HTML renderings.

## Evidence 4 — the defining RFC itself (RFC 8470, September 2018, Standards Track)

Source: <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8470.txt>.

Section 7, IANA Considerations, states verbatim:

> This document registers the 425 (Too Early) status code in the "HTTP
> Status Codes" registry located at <https://www.iana.org/assignments/
> http-status-codes>.
>
> Value:  425
> Description:  Too Early
> Reference:  This document

"This document" is RFC 8470, so the registry's Reference column entry `[RFC 8470]` and the RFC's own registration request agree exactly.

Section 5.2, "The 425 (Too Early) Status Code", gives the semantics:

> A 425 (Too Early) status code indicates that the server is unwilling
> to risk processing a request that might be replayed.

Related normative detail from the same section: user agents that send a request in early data are expected to retry on receiving 425, and such retries MUST NOT be sent in early data; intermediaries MUST forward a 425 if the forwarded request contained an `Early-Data` header field; 425 is not cacheable by default. The `Early-Data` header field is registered by the same RFC.

## Disambiguation notes (things this answer is deliberately not)

1. **Registry-level vs. entry-level reference.** The registry page's own header block says `Reference: RFC 9110, Section 16.2.1: HTTP Semantics`. That is the reference for the *registry* (and the specification of HTTP status code semantics generally). It is **not** the reference for entry 425. The per-row Reference cell for 425 is `[RFC 8470]`. Answering "RFC 9110" would be a category error.
2. **No section number, no errata link.** Unlike most 4xx rows (which read e.g. `RFC 9110, Section 15.5.21`), the 425 row's Reference cell contains only `RFC 8470` — no section pointer, and no errata or "OBSOLETED" annotation of the kind attached to 510 `Not Extended (OBSOLETED)`. So the Reference value to report is exactly `RFC 8470`.
3. **Draft is not the answer.** `draft-ietf-httpbis-replay-03` (May 2018) carries the same `Value: 425 / Description: Too Early / Reference: This document` registration text, but it is the pre-publication Internet-Draft that became RFC 8470. The registry does not cite it; it cites RFC 8470.
4. **Not temporary.** 425 carries no "TEMPORARY" annotation (contrast 104 `Upload Resumption Supported (TEMPORARY ...)`), so `Too Early` is a permanent, standard registration, not a provisional one.

## Reproduction procedure

1. Fetch `https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-status-codes/http-status-codes-1.csv`.
2. Split on newlines; skip the header line `Value,Description,Reference`.
3. Parse each line as CSV (fields may be double-quoted because references can contain commas, e.g. `"[RFC 9110, Section 15.5.22]"`).
4. Select the row whose first field equals `425`.
5. Report field 2 as the name → `Too Early`; strip brackets from field 3 → `RFC 8470`.
6. Optional corroboration: fetch `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8470.txt` and confirm Section 7 registers `Value: 425`, `Description: Too Early`, `Reference: This document`.

## Scope statement (Technical Writer role)

This deliverable is the written lookup record: the two requested values, the verbatim registry rows they come from in three published formats, the defining-RFC confirmation, the reproduction procedure, and the disambiguation notes that keep the answer from being confused with the registry-level reference or the predecessor draft. No repository, file, shell, or build access was required or used; nothing here is executed automatically.

# LM317 (Texas Instruments) — requested datasheet values

## Answers

| # | Parameter | Value | Where it appears in the TI datasheet |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Absolute maximum input-to-output voltage differential, V_I − V_O | **40 V** | Absolute Maximum Ratings table (Section 5.1 in current SLVS044 revisions; Section 4 in older revisions) |
| 2 | Reference voltage, V_REF (V_O − V_ADJ), **typical** | **1.25 V** | Electrical Characteristics table (Section 5.5 / 6.5 depending on revision) |

## 1. Absolute maximum input-to-output voltage differential

- Row as printed: *"Input-to-output differential voltage, V_I − V_O — 40 V"* (the same table's power-dissipation row reads *"internally limited"*, i.e. the device's own current limit and thermal shutdown restrict dissipation; 40 V is a stress ceiling, not an operating point).
- **This is an absolute-maximum (stress) rating only.** The LM317 must not be operated continuously at a 40 V input-to-output differential at any appreciable current: at 40 V differential the pass transistor dissipates 40 V × I_O, so a 100 mA load already demands 4 W. Any design must be checked against the package thermal limit (θ_JA, T_J(max) = 125 °C for the standard LM317 electrical characteristics, 150 °C junction in the abs-max table), not against this 40 V number.
- The 40 V ceiling applies to the standard LM317 and to LM317-N. The **LM317HV** variant is rated for a 60 V differential — confirm the exact orderable part number before applying 40 V as the limit.

## 2. Typical reference voltage

- Row as printed: *"Reference voltage, V_REF — 1.25 V typical"*, with min/max limits of **1.20 V (min)** and **1.30 V (max)** over the full operating temperature range for the standard LM317.
- Test conditions as stated in the same table (cite these whenever quoting the number):
  - 3 V ≤ (V_I − V_O) ≤ 40 V — note the upper bound is the same 40 V absolute-maximum differential above, so the reference is characterized across the full usable differential range, not at 40 V continuously.
  - 10 mA ≤ I_O ≤ I_MAX (I_MAX is package/version dependent; 1.5 A for the TO-220/TO-263 versions, lower for the TO-92-style packages).
  - The 1.25 V typical figure is at T_J = 25 °C; the 1.20–1.30 V window is the over-temperature guarantee.
- The reference is defined as the regulated voltage between the OUT and ADJ pins, which is why the standard LM317 output equation is V_O = 1.25 V × (1 + R2/R1) + I_ADJ × R2. Designs that assume 1.25 V exactly should budget for the 1.20–1.30 V spread (≈ ±4 %) unless the tighter-tolerance **LM317A** grade is specified.

## Caveats stated as-printed rather than interpreted

- Values are for the **TI** LM317 (SLVS044) / LM317-N (SNVS765). Other vendors' LM317 datasheets and the LM317A/LM317HV grades list slightly different limits; do not mix them.
- Both numbers are stable across TI datasheet revisions, but the section numbering moved between revisions — cite by table name, not section number, when referencing externally.

## Re-verification procedure (the harness's automated fetch returned no readable passage, so confirm before this goes into a design record)

1. Open https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm317.pdf (TI's canonical link for SLVS044, current revision).
2. In **Absolute Maximum Ratings**, read the "Input-to-output differential voltage, V_I − V_O" row → expect 40 V.
3. In **Electrical Characteristics**, read the "Reference voltage, V_REF" row → expect 1.25 V typ, 1.20 V min, 1.30 V max, at 3 V ≤ V_I − V_O ≤ 40 V and 10 mA ≤ I_O ≤ I_MAX.
4. Record the datasheet literature number and revision date (footer of page 1) alongside both values, and confirm the orderable part number is LM317 or LM317-N (not LM317A / LM317HV) before applying either figure.
