answer:
ANSWER (14 CFR § 91.151, current text, U.S. jurisdiction)

A glider is required to carry NO fuel reserve to begin a flight under VFR conditions. Numerically: 0 minutes. Section 91.151 imposes no fuel-reserve requirement on gliders at all, because neither of its two operative paragraphs reaches them.

1. THE REGULATION, VERBATIM

14 CFR § 91.151 — Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions:

"(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.

(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

Source: eCFR, 14 CFR 91.151 (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-91/subpart-B/subject-group-ECFR4d7cd0e3cc4be86/section-91.151), and the 2026 CFR print at 14 CFR part 91 / sec. 91.151 (govinfo, CFR-2026-title14-vol2). The text is identical in all sources reviewed; the section carries no amendment note later than the base text and contains no glider provision.

2. WHY GLIDERS ARE OUTSIDE § 91.151 — TEXTUAL CHAIN

Step 1 — The rule is category-specific, not aircraft-wide. § 91.151 contains exactly two prohibitions, each keyed to a named category: 'an airplane' in (a) and 'a rotorcraft' in (b). There is no residual clause, no 'other aircraft,' and no glider paragraph. Where the FAA wanted a category-specific reserve it named the category and gave it its own number (20 minutes for rotorcraft, against 30/45 for airplanes). A glider falls in neither sentence, so neither prohibition can be violated by a glider.

Step 2 — Part 1 definitions confirm a glider is not an 'airplane.' 14 CFR § 1.1:
• "Airplane means an engine-driven fixed-wing aircraft heavier than air, that is supported in flight by the dynamic reaction of the air against its wings."
• "Glider means a heavier-than-air aircraft, that is supported in flight by the dynamic reaction of the air against its lifting surfaces and whose free flight does not depend principally on an engine."
A glider is therefore a separate regulatory category, not a sub-type of airplane. Reading 'airplane' in § 91.151(a) to include gliders would contradict the Part 1 definition and would also make the rotorcraft-specific paragraph (b) incoherent as a drafting scheme.

Step 3 — Part 91's general applicability does not fill the gap. § 91.1(a) makes Part 91 apply broadly to 'the operation of aircraft,' but general applicability only puts an aircraft inside the Part; it does not expand the subject of a specific section. Section 91.151's subject is limited by its own words to airplanes and rotorcraft. (The same drafting pattern appears elsewhere in Part 91, e.g. § 91.213(d)(1)(i), which lists 'glider' as its own category alongside 'non-turbine-powered airplane' — the FAA consistently treats gliders as a distinct class.)

Step 4 — Result. No fuel reserve figure is imposed on a glider by § 91.151. Answer: none (0 minutes). The 30-minute day and 45-minute night figures are airplane figures; the 20-minute figure is a rotorcraft figure. None of the three applies to a glider.

3. WHAT DOES APPLY TO A GLIDER INSTEAD (so the answer is not read as 'no planning required')

• § 91.103 — Preflight action. The PIC must 'become familiar with all available information concerning that flight,' including fuel requirements for a flight not in the vicinity of an airport. For a glider, the operative planning quantity is altitude/glide energy, not fuel volume. This is the section that actually obliges the glider pilot to plan a margin; it prescribes no number.
• § 91.119 — Minimum safe altitudes. Applies to all aircraft; the 'emergency landing without undue hazard' standard is the closest regulatory analogue to a reserve for an unpowered aircraft.
• § 91.155 — Basic VFR weather minimums; § 91.113 — right-of-way; § 91.209 — lights (relevant if anyone contemplates night flight).
• No FAA rule sets a numeric altitude or 'glide margin' reserve for gliders. Club, contest and site rules (e.g., minimum pattern-entry altitude, final-glide margin) are private standards, not § 91.151.

4. MOTORGLIDERS / SELF-LAUNCHERS — DECISION RULE

The applicability question is the aircraft's certificated category, not whether it has an engine.
• If the aircraft is type certificated in the glider category (self-launching or touring motorglider, including light-sport gliders), § 91.151 by its terms does not apply, even when the engine is running. Advisory practice (NOT a regulation): flight-plan the engine fuel exactly as if § 91.151(a) applied — 30 min day / 45 min night at normal cruising speed after the first point of intended landing — because a sustainer engine that runs dry converts the flight into a pure glider flight with no declared reserve. Worked example: normal cruise 90 kt, 4 gph. 30 min = 45 nm = 2.0 gal; 45 min = 67.5 nm = 3.0 gal. Carry that on top of fuel to the first point of intended landing.
• If the aircraft is type certificated as an airplane (some motorgliders are), § 91.151(a) applies in full: enough fuel to the first point of intended landing plus 30 min day / 45 min night at normal cruising speed.

5. NIGHT VFR

The 45-minute night reserve in § 91.151(a)(2) is an airplane provision and does not reach gliders. A glider operating at night would still need to satisfy § 91.209 lighting and § 91.155 VFR minimums; it acquires no fuel-reserve obligation from § 91.151 either way.

6. ADVISORY (clearly non-regulatory) — the glider analogue of a reserve

Because a glider's reserve is altitude, the operationally meaningful planning figure is a glide margin to the intended landing area. Illustration: a 15:1 glider at 3,000 ft AGL above the intended touchdown has 3,000 × 15 = 45,000 ft of still-air glide = 45,000 / 6,076.12 = 7.41 nm. Prudent practice is to plan arrival at pattern/landing height with a stated surplus (commonly expressed in club or contest rules as a required finish altitude) rather than to consume the full computed glide. This paragraph is airmanship guidance only; it creates no legal requirement and is not § 91.151.

7. SCOPE / QUALIFICATIONS

• Jurisdiction assumed: United States, 14 CFR. Operations under a foreign code (e.g., EASA Part-NCO) are outside this answer and must be checked against that code; this answer does not state any non-U.S. figure.

• Bottom line for the record: glider, VFR, § 91.151 — required fuel reserve: none (0 minutes).

question: H16
answer:
ANSWER

A trucker may drive up to 8 cumulative hours before a break is required. Once 8 cumulative hours of driving time have passed without at least one consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status, the driver may not drive again until they take a qualifying break of at least 30 consecutive minutes. (In short: 8 hours of driving -> 30-minute break.)

SCOPE / ASSUMPTION THIS ANSWER RESTS ON

This is the US federal rule for property-carrying commercial motor vehicle drivers under FMCSA Hours of Service, 49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii). Hours-of-service law is jurisdiction-specific, and the number differs elsewhere; the grounding for this answer covers the US federal property-carrying rule only. If the driver is a passenger carrier, the answer changes (see 'Exceptions and variants' below).

REGULATORY BASIS (verbatim)

49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii): 'Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in Sec. 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. A consecutive 30-minute interruption of driving status may be satisfied either by off-duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving time or by a combination of off-duty, sleeper berth and on-duty not driving time.'

FMCSA summary of the rule: 'Drivers must take a 30-minute break when they have driven for a period of 8 cumulative hours without at least a 30-minute interruption.'

HOW THE 8 HOURS ARE COUNTED

1. It is CUMULATIVE driving time, not consecutive. Short stops, fuel stops, paperwork, loading/unloading, or any non-driving period shorter than 30 consecutive minutes do not reset the 8-hour clock. Only a single uninterrupted block of at least 30 consecutive minutes in a non-driving status resets it to zero.
2. All driving in the work period counts toward the 8 hours, regardless of how it is broken up, and regardless of how many motor carriers the driver is working for.
3. The break must be taken BEFORE the driver exceeds 8 hours of driving without an interruption - i.e., the driver may drive up to 8 hours, then must stop driving and take the break.
4. The break does not pause or extend the 14-hour on-duty window: 'Off-duty time does not extend the 14-hour period.' Break time is charged against the 14-hour window even though it resets the 8-hour break clock.

WHAT QUALIFIES AS THE BREAK

A consecutive 30 minutes (or more) of any of the following, or any consecutive combination of them:
- off-duty time,
- sleeper berth time,
- on-duty not driving time.

Practical consequence: a driver does not have to be off duty to satisfy the rule - 30 consecutive minutes of on-duty not-driving (e.g., waiting at a dock, fueling, paperwork) satisfies it.

WORKED EXAMPLE

06:00 - comes on duty (14-hour window runs to 20:00).
06:00-10:00 - drives 4.0 h. Cumulative driving = 4.0 h.
10:00-10:20 - on-duty not driving, 20 minutes. Under 30 minutes, so it does NOT reset the break clock.
10:20-14:20 - drives 4.0 h. Cumulative driving = 8.0 h. The 8-hour trigger is now reached.
14:20 - driver may NOT drive further until a qualifying break is taken.
14:20-14:50 - 30 consecutive minutes off duty / sleeper berth / on-duty not driving. Break clock resets to zero.
14:50-17:50 - may drive up to 3.0 more hours: 8.0 h already driven, 11-hour driving limit leaves 3.0 h; and 17:50 is inside the 20:00 end of the 14-hour window.

Check against every limit used above: total driving 11.0 h = the 11-hour maximum (not exceeded); all driving ends 17:50, before the 20:00 end of the 14-hour window; the 30-minute break is exactly the 30-minute minimum; the 20-minute stop correctly fails to reset the clock.

LIMITS OFTEN CONFUSED WITH THIS ONE (property-carrying drivers)

| Limit | Value | What it governs |
|---|---|---|
| Break trigger | 8 cumulative hours of driving | When the 30-minute break is required (this answer) |
| Break length | 30 consecutive minutes minimum | What satisfies the break |
| Driving limit | 11 hours | Total driving permitted within the 14-hour window |
| On-duty window | 14 consecutive hours after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty | Latest time driving may occur; off-duty time does not extend it |
| Weekly limit | 60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days (carrier not operating every day) / 70 hours in 8 consecutive days (operating every day) | Weekly on-duty cap |
| Restart | 34 or more consecutive hours off duty | Restarts the 7/8-day period |
| Adverse driving conditions | Up to 2 additional hours on the driving limit and window (16-hour window / up to 13 hours driving) | Extends the 11-hour and 14-hour limits when adverse conditions are encountered |
| Short-haul exception | Within 150 air-miles of the normal work reporting location, duty period not exceeding 14 hours | Drivers meeting 395.1(e)(1)/(2) are excepted from the break requirement (and from 395.8/395.11 records requirements) |

So: 8 hours is the break trigger. It is NOT the daily driving limit (that is 11 hours), and it is not the on-duty window (that is 14 hours).

EXCEPTIONS AND VARIANTS

- Short-haul drivers. By the express terms of 395.3(a)(3)(ii), drivers who qualify for the short-haul exceptions in 395.1(e)(1) or (2) are excepted from the 8-hour/30-minute break requirement. Those exceptions require operating within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location and reporting and returning within 14 consecutive hours, with a maximum duty period of 14 hours.
- Passenger-carrying vehicles. Different limits apply: 10-hour driving limit after 8 consecutive hours off duty, and a 15-hour on-duty limit after 8 consecutive hours off duty. FMCSA's visor card describes the 30-minute break as a requirement 'for property carriers only,' so the 8-hour figure should not be carried over to passenger carriers without checking 49 CFR 395.5.
- Adverse driving conditions. The grounded sources describe the adverse-conditions exception as extending the driving limit and the on-duty window (by up to 2 hours). They do not state that it extends the 8-hour break trigger, so no extension of the 8-hour figure is asserted here; treat any such extension as unverified against this grounding.
- Sleeper-berth split. The property-carrier sleeper-berth provision allows the required 10 hours off duty to be split into two periods (one at least 2 hours, the other at least 7 consecutive hours in the berth, totaling at least 10 hours), and neither period counts against the 14-hour window when used together. This affects the 10-hour/14-hour structure, not the 8-hour break trigger itself.
- Non-US jurisdictions (EU, Canada, etc.) have their own break rules and different numbers. This answer does not address them.

ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR THE DRIVER

Drive no more than 8 cumulative hours without a break; before driving past the 8th hour, take at least 30 consecutive minutes off driving (off duty, sleeper berth, or on-duty not driving), and remember that break time still burns your 14-hour window and your total driving for the shift is capped at 11 hours.
